title: What Is Mine Cage/Hoist? — Definition
body:
Building and digging before hydraulics: block and tackle, gin poles and derricks, steam shovels (Marion, Bucyrus), horse-drawn scrapers, picks and ore carts, stamp mills and arrastras, assay offices, and the powder monkeys' world of historical mining and construction.

title: Origins and History of Mine Cage/Hoist
body:
The Mine Cage/Hoist belongs to the 1800s–1980s era and traces to Various.

Block and tackle rigged pyramids' descendants for millennia; the gin pole raised barns and derricks raised cities. Steam shovels (Otis, 1839; Marion, Bucyrus) dug the Panama Canal; horse-drawn Fresno scrapers graded the West. Hard-rock mining used hand steel (single/double jack), then machine drills; stamp mills crushed ore and arrastras ground it with mule power. The assay office decided fortunes. Dynamite (Nobel, 1867) replaced black powder; the hydraulic excavator (1950s) finally retired the cable shovel for most work.

Within that longer story, Mine Cage/Hoist: The 1800s; the 1900s'. The cage is the shaft's lift.

title: How Mine Cage/Hoist Works
body:
Block and tackle trade rope length for force: each supporting rope divides the load. Derricks and gin poles are lever-cranes stabilized by guy lines. Steam shovels crowd a dipper into the bank with cables and rack teeth, then swing and dump. Stamp mills drop heavy stamps on ore in mortars, washing pulp over amalgamation plates; arrastras drag stones in a circle. Assaying fire-tests samples: cupellation separates precious metals from lead. Black powder and dynamite fracture rock; drilling patterns control the break.

Applied to the Mine Cage/Hoist (1800s–1980s, Various): The cage is the shaft's lift.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Construction and Mining History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of construction and mining history:

• mechanical advantage — Ropes supporting the load divide it.
• crowd — Forcing the dipper into the bank.
• bank / face — The digging front.
• muck — Broken rock to move.
• single jack / double jack — One- or two-handed hammer drilling.
• stamp mill — Gravity-stamp ore crusher.
• arrastra — Drag-stone grinding mill.
• amalgamation — Mercury catching gold/silver.
• cupellation — Fire assay separating precious metals.
• powder monkey — The blaster's helper; the dangerous job.

The steam shovel is the industrial dinosaur children never outgrow; 'Mike Mulligan' is literature. Gold-rush stamp mills still thunder for tourists. Powder monkeys and muckers are labor history's heroes; the assay office decided boom or bust. Every sandbox excavator descends from Marion.

title: Mine Cage/Hoist Restoration Guide
body:
Cable machines: inspect wire rope and drums; repack glands. Boilers need certification. Preserve, don't over-restore — working patina tells the story.

Restoration order for a Mine Cage/Hoist: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision.
